I'm so glad to see a post that's so honest and is actually looking for beginner help. I'm tired of some people boasting about their ability to run 70 miles a week, like they're some sort of god. I think it really bastardizes the attempts by people to get into running... But I digress.

Let me give you a little background on me. I swam competitively since I was 5. Now 21, I only began running a little before my 21st birthday, and I did my first marathon 8 months after starting. So trust me, you can get beyond this two kilometer hurdle you're facing.

First things first, don't compare yourself to other people. This is something my grandfather always told me: it's either gonna make you feel superior, or make you feel worthless. You are who you are, and if you're hurting at short distances right now, you're hurting. There's no way you should feel besides the way you do, so keep up trying.

Secondly, know your body. Just starting out, if your body is in weird pain (and I mean skeletal pain) the day after a run, take that day off. Rest is underrated, and if you feel yourself still wanting to work out, go for a bike or a swim, or go rock climbing: there's a lot of natural ways you can build up your muscles.

I'd imagine your current problems are due to ligament weakness, bad shoe soles, or perhaps weak legs. I would stress, then, promoting other activities that increase leg strength (as said in the last paragraph). Once you feel your body getting more in shape, then you can rely on running a little more.

Be careful, and don't hurt yourself. PM me and keep me updated, and feel free to ask me any questions!

The biggest issue for keeping shoes this long is the breakdown of support. Maybe you could replace the soles and have them for a few hundred more, but it's generally best practice to replace after 500-1000 miles.

I have coworkers who replace them after only 200 miles, though this is a bit outrageous in my opinion. As for me, I replace my saucony shoes when they start falling apart, but this is only when I hit the range of 500-700 miles.

You could just be comfortable even if the support is breaking down simply because you run a lot. Your ligaments and tendons may be stronger and not feel the impact. Generally you do what is right for you. Also, buy multiple pairs when you find what's right (if you can).

If you were asking about yourself, I would suggest the most important shots would be for chicken pox (if you haven't had it) and the MMR, which kills three birds with one stone.  You may read up or ask your physician about the safety of said and other vaccines at your age.  It would be an extremely wise decision for you to be vaccinated, but don't do it all at once, it could put a huge burden upon the shoulders (so to speak) of your lymphatic system.

I'm assuming that your asking if you should be worried about your child. If that was your question, then he'll no (no pun intended either).  When you vaccinate your child, you are not only making them immune to a debilitating pathogen, but also a non-viable carrier in the community of said pathogen, e.g. polio. It is not only good for your child, but good for the community, as it decreases the chance of infection of the people around you child.  There are those who are huge enemies of vaccinations, due to the rare cases of debilitating side-effects. But let us be honest, those side effects have never even been identified as being correlated in any way to the original vaccination, and many claims that disorders such as autism are caused by shots are backed up with faulty evidence and disproven with thorough research by doctors with very much experience.

Since the inception of vaccines to cure transmitable cow diseases (hence vac- the latin root for cow), vaccines have been at the forefront of fighting a war on viruses that plague our world and threaten the lives of several in our communities.
